subsection: 12. Nazi propaganda; case study: the Nuremberg Rallies

notes.h: Nazi propaganda: setting, aims and methods
notes.b: Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, and the regime soon treated control of what Germans read, heard and saw as a main tool of rule. Understanding what the propaganda was for, and which ideas it repeated, explains the choices made in every medium that follows.
points: By mid-1933 Germany was a one-party state, so the regime could use the whole machinery of government to push its message.
Propaganda is the organised spreading of ideas, images and information to shape opinion and win loyalty to a regime, its leader and its policies.
Its aims were to win and keep consent, build the Hitler cult, create the national community, spread racial ideas and prepare Germans for rearmament and war.

A personality cult presents the leader as an infallible, heroic saviour of the nation through propaganda, ritual and his image in daily life. For Hitler it was known as the Hitler cult or 'Führer myth'.

The same core ideas were repeated: the national community (Volksgemeinschaft, one united German people), the leader principle (all authority flows from Hitler), anti-communism, anti-Semitism, the 'shame' of the Treaty of Versailles, and the glory of the German nation.

Methods were simple themes repeated constantly, because repetition makes slogans stick, emotional appeal rather than argument, the mixing of entertainment with political messages, and the use of every new medium. Posters, parades, slogans and mass rallies bound people to the leader and the party.

Totalitarianism means a state that seeks to control all public and private life through one party, secret police, terror and propaganda. Control of the mass media and culture was one of its main tools.
Propaganda worked alongside terror (the Gestapo, the camps and the courts): persuasion won over the willing, while fear silenced those who could not be persuaded.
notes.tip: Exam questions on propaganda and terror reward you for pairing a propaganda method with a terror method and judging which kept the dictator in power. Use named institutions and dates, such as the ministry of 1933, the Volksempfänger and the rallies.

notes.h: State control of culture: the Ministry and the Reich Chamber of Culture
notes.b: The Nazis did not leave the media to chance. They set up one government ministry to direct them and a compulsory membership body to decide who was allowed to work in them.
points: The Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda was established by decree on 13 March 1933 with Joseph Goebbels as minister (1933-1945). It took charge of the press, radio, film, theatre, music and the arts, so one man gave the orders for all of them.

Gleichschaltung ('coordination') of culture means bringing the press, radio, film and the arts into line with Nazi ideology. Here the term is used only for culture, not for the wider takeover of the state.
The Reich Chamber of Culture was created by a law of September 1933, with Goebbels as president. It had sub-chambers for the press, radio, film, music, theatre, fine arts and literature.
Anyone working in these fields, including writers, painters, musicians and actors, had to be admitted to the chamber. Jews and opponents were excluded, so exclusion meant losing one's livelihood.
notes.tip: Keep the three bodies apart. The Ministry of Propaganda (March 1933) was a government department, the Reich Chamber of Culture (September 1933) was a compulsory membership body, and the Reich Film Chamber (1933) was one part of that system.

notes.b: Newspapers were the first medium to be brought into line. The regime did this by making editors answerable to the state, telling them daily what to print, and buying out independent owners.
points: The Editors' Law of October 1933 made editors responsible to the state and barred Jews, so Jewish journalists were excluded from the press.
The Reich Press Chamber and the ministry's daily press conferences told papers what to print and how to present it, so newspapers across the country carried the same line.
Max Amann, head of the party publishing house (the Eher Verlag), bought up or closed independent papers, which put much of the press in party hands.

Three papers are easy to confuse: the Völkischer Beobachter was the party daily, Der Angriff ('The Attack') was Goebbels's Berlin paper founded in 1927, and Der Stürmer was Julius Streicher's anti-Semitic weekly.
notes.tip: Name the Editors' Law with its key point, editors responsible to the state and Jews barred, rather than saying only that editors had to join approved organisations.

notes.h: Radio: the People's Receiver and wartime control
notes.b: Radio could carry Hitler's voice into every home, so the regime took it over early and then made sure ordinary families could afford a set.
points: Broadcasting was taken under the ministry's control in 1933 when the ministry took over the broadcasting companies, so every programme could be vetted.
The Volksempfänger (People's Receiver) was a cheap radio set launched at the Berlin radio exhibition in August 1933 and priced at 76 Reichsmarks, so that ordinary households could buy one.
Loudspeakers in factories, offices and squares allowed communal listening to major speeches, so people without a set still heard the leaders.
Programmes mixed light music and entertainment with speeches and news. This kept people listening, and the political message reached them along with the music.
From September 1939 listening to foreign stations such as the BBC was a crime with heavy penalties, and some people were executed for spreading what they had heard.
notes.tip: Cinema and radio questions want you to show how the medium was used, not just list it. For radio, link the People's Receiver (cheap sets), loudspeakers (communal listening) and the wartime ban to the aim of controlling what people heard.

notes.b: Cinema was the most popular medium, so the regime controlled the film industry closely and used it to carry both entertainment and propaganda.
points: The Reich Film Chamber (1933) controlled the industry. Scripts were vetted, films the regime judged unsuitable were banned, and the state funded films with propaganda messages.
Most feature films were entertainment, but every programme carried a newsreel. Audiences who came for the entertainment therefore also received the regime's version of events.
From 1940 a single newsreel, the Deutsche Wochenschau, was shown across occupied Europe, so the same view of the war reached audiences in conquered countries.
Hitler Youth Quex (Hitlerjunge Quex, 1933) was an early propaganda film that glorified the movement's young followers.
Jud Süß (1940, directed by Veit Harlan) and The Eternal Jew (Der ewige Jude, 1940) were explicit anti-Semitic propaganda. Jud Süß was shown to audiences in Germany and occupied countries.
Kolberg (1945, also directed by Veit Harlan) was a costly late-war film about resistance to the end, made to stiffen morale when the war was being lost.
notes.tip: When a question asks about film as a mass medium, explain how it was used (vetting, newsreels in every programme, entertainment carrying a message) and use the films as evidence, rather than listing titles.

notes.h: Posters, slogans and the Hitler cult in daily life
notes.b: Alongside the big media, the regime filled everyday life with signs of loyalty to the leader. This is how the Hitler cult reached people who never went to a rally.
points: Posters and slogans were widely displayed. 'Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer' (one people, one empire, one leader) was used around the Anschluss of 1938 and packed the regime's message into five words.
The 'Heil Hitler' greeting made an everyday exchange into a small act of loyalty to the leader, so refusing it stood out.

Hitler's portrait hung in public places, his birthday on 20 April was a public celebration, and books of photographs by Heinrich Hoffmann, his personal photographer, showed him as the saviour and father of the nation.
Youth and women's organisations, schools and the Labour Front (the state-run body for workers) were used for indoctrination, so people met the same ideas at school, at work and in their free time.

notes.h: Book burning, degenerate art and music
notes.b: Controlling culture meant not only promoting approved work but also destroying and condemning anything that did not fit Nazi ideology. Public spectacles made the condemnation part of the propaganda.
points: On 10 May 1933, organised by the German Student Union, students and party members burned books by Jewish, Marxist, liberal and pacifist authors on the Opernplatz in Berlin and in other university towns. Goebbels spoke in Berlin.
Authors whose books were burned included Karl Marx, Sigmund Freud, Erich Maria Remarque (author of All Quiet on the Western Front) and Heinrich Heine, so the burning targeted ideas the regime feared.
Heine had written in 1821: 'Where they burn books, they will in the end burn people too.' The line is now inscribed at the book-burning memorial in Berlin, and it belongs to Heine, not to Goebbels.
Degenerate art was the Nazi label for modern art such as Expressionism and abstract art, which was condemned and removed from galleries.
The Degenerate Art (Entartete Kunst) exhibition opened in Munich in July 1937, the day after the Great German Art Exhibition of approved art opened in the new House of German Art.
It showed modernist works, including those by Otto Dix, George Grosz, Emil Nolde, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Paul Klee, as examples of decadence.

The Degenerate Art exhibition drew about two million visitors, far more than the approved exhibition beside it, so the regime's attempt to teach people to despise modern art was also a very popular show.
In music, jazz was condemned as 'degenerate' and works by Jewish composers were banned.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two Munich exhibitions of July 1937: the Degenerate Art exhibition (condemned modern art) and the Great German Art Exhibition (approved art).

notes.h: The 1936 Olympics as a propaganda showcase
notes.b: Hosting the Olympics gave the regime a world audience. It used the Games to present a peaceful, modern and efficient Germany to foreign visitors.
points: The Winter Games were held at Garmisch-Partenkirchen in February 1936 and the Summer Games in Berlin in August 1936, so say which Games you mean.
The regime wanted visitors to see a peaceful, modern, efficient Germany, and it removed anti-Semitic signs for the games so that foreign guests would not meet open racial hatred.

At the Summer Games in Berlin, Germany won the most medals (about 89, ahead of the USA), which the regime used as proof of national strength. At the Winter Games Norway, not Germany, topped the medal table.
Jesse Owens (USA) won four gold medals. His success was a limit on the racial message, because the regime claimed that some races were superior to others.
notes.tip: Never write that Germany 'won the most medals' in 1936 without saying which Games: it is true only of the Summer Games in Berlin.

notes.b: In war the aim of propaganda changed from celebrating success to holding the home front together. The message had to shift when the news turned bad.
points: In the early years of the war, victories were celebrated in the newsreels, which fed the idea that Hitler and the army were unbeatable.
After the German surrender at Stalingrad in early February 1943, the message shifted to endurance and fear of the enemy, because victory could no longer be promised.

On 18 February 1943 Goebbels gave his total war speech at the Berlin Sportpalast, asking the crowd 'Do you want total war?' (Wollt ihr den totalen Krieg?). It was broadcast nationally so that the whole country heard the call.
As defeats mounted, the credibility of propaganda declined, because people could compare the official claims with what they saw and heard around them.
notes.tip: Keep the total war speech (February 1943) apart from Goebbels's post as Plenipotentiary for Total War (July 1944): the speech came first and the post followed seventeen months later.

notes.b: Goebbels was the Gauleiter (party leader) of Berlin and then the head of Nazi propaganda from 1933 to 1945. He directed the machine that controlled what Germans saw and heard.
points: Born in 1897 in Rheydt, Rhineland, he had a club foot that kept him out of the First World War army. He gained a doctorate in literature (Heidelberg, 1921) and failed as a writer. In the mid-1920s he joined the party on Strasser's 'socialist' northern wing, until Hitler won him over in 1926.

Hitler made him Gauleiter of Berlin in November 1926. There he organised street fights with the communists, mass meetings and his paper Der Angriff (from 1927), and he made Horst Wessel, an SA man killed in 1930, a martyr whose song became the party anthem.

From 1930 he was party propaganda chief (Reich Propaganda Leader). He ran the Reichstag campaigns of 1930 and 1932 and the presidential campaign of 1932, in which Hitler flew across Germany, using posters, films, records, loudspeaker vans and radio.

As Minister of Propaganda from March 1933 he also headed the Reich Chamber of Culture and organised the book burning. His anti-Semitic films and his Munich speech of 9 November 1938, which encouraged the Kristallnacht pogrom, show his role.

In the war he gave the total war speech (1943) and became Plenipotentiary for Total War in July 1944. Hitler's will named him Reich Chancellor, and on 1 May 1945, the day after Hitler's suicide, he and his wife Magda killed their six children and then themselves in Berlin.

He was a participant who directed the propaganda machine rather than a witness to events. He claimed the creation of the Führer myth as his greatest achievement, and his diaries are a major source for historians.

Contemporaries saw a brilliant, cynical speaker and organiser who stayed loyal to Hitler. Rivals in the leadership, Göring, Himmler, Ribbentrop and Rosenberg, disliked and distrusted him, which is why his power over culture was never complete.

Historians judge him the most skilled propagandist of the age, but argue that propaganda worked best when it reinforced existing beliefs (nationalism, anti-communism, the Hitler cult) and less well when it tried to change them. His influence fell in the late 1930s and rose again from 1943.
notes.tip: Learn Goebbels's three posts and dates: Gauleiter of Berlin (1926), Minister of Propaganda (1933) and Plenipotentiary for Total War (1944). Do not confuse him with Göring (Four Year Plan) or Himmler (SS).

notes.b: Born in Berlin in 1902, Riefenstahl trained as a dancer, acted in 'mountain films' and directed and starred in The Blue Light (1932). She admired Hitler and met him in 1932, and her rally and Olympic films gave the regime its most lasting images.
points: Hitler, not Goebbels, commissioned her to film the rallies, with a large crew; she and Goebbels were on poor terms. Her films were Victory of Faith (1933 rally), Triumph of the Will (released 1935, 1934 rally) and Day of Freedom (1935, the army at the 1935 rally).

Victory of Faith was withdrawn after the murder of Ernst Röhm in 1934. Triumph of the Will opens with Hitler's aeroplane descending through clouds over Nuremberg and uses moving cameras, low angles, no narrator and music by Herbert Windt.
Triumph of the Will sets the leader against massed ranks, which gives its message of unity behind Hitler after the purge and shows Hitler and the party as the sole leadership.

Her documentary Olympia (1938) covers the 1936 Berlin Olympics in two parts, Festival of the Nations and Festival of Beauty. Its new camera techniques (underwater, tracking and slow motion) presented athletic achievement as a national triumph. It premiered on 20 April 1938, Hitler's birthday.

Contemporaries praised her art. Triumph of the Will won the German National Film Prize in 1935 and a gold medal at the Paris World Exhibition in 1937, and foreign audiences admired the films as cinema, while critics abroad recognised their propaganda purpose.

During the war she made Tiefland, for which Sinti and Roma were taken from an internment camp as extras; it was released in 1954. After 1945 she was interned and, after several denazification hearings, was classified as a 'fellow traveller' (Mitläufer), not a major offender.
She always claimed her films were art or documentary, not propaganda, and that she knew nothing of the regime's crimes. She later photographed the Nuba of Sudan and died in 2003, aged 101.

She was a willing participant who gave the regime its most lasting images. Historians and critics judge her films technically brilliant and influential but reject her claim to be non-political, as Susan Sontag did in her 1975 essay 'Fascinating Fascism', and they still debate the line between art and propaganda.
notes.tip: Expect 'who made Triumph of the Will and what did it record': Riefenstahl, and the 1934 rally. Keep her films apart: Victory of Faith (1933 rally, withdrawn), Triumph of the Will (1934 rally), Day of Freedom (army, 1935) and Olympia (1936 Games, released 1938).

notes.h: Case study background: the rallies and why Nuremberg
notes.b: The Nuremberg Rallies were the Nazi party's yearly show of strength. Nuremberg was chosen for the setting because of what the city stood for and because it suited huge gatherings.
points: The Reichsparteitag (Reich party congress, or rally) was the party's annual gathering. Do not confuse it with the Reichstag, the parliament.
Earlier rallies were held in Munich (1923) and Weimar (1926). The party then met in Nuremberg in August 1927 and 1929, and every September from 1933 to 1938, each rally lasting about a week.

Nuremberg was a medieval free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire and a symbol of German history and greatness. The Nazis used its old buildings and traditions to link the Third Reich to the First (the Holy Roman Empire).
Practical reasons also counted: it had a central position and good railway links, the local party under Julius Streicher (Gauleiter of Franconia) was strong, and there was open land for vast grounds.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Nuremberg Rallies (party congresses, 1927-1938), the Nuremberg Laws (15 September 1935) and the Nuremberg trials (1945-46).

notes.h: Case study: the rally grounds and staging
notes.b: The grounds were built to turn the rallies into a spectacle of order and power, and they were designed around the Dutzendteich lake, away from the old city.
points: The grounds lay south-east of the city, around the Dutzendteich lake, on open land that could hold vast crowds.
The Luitpold Arena was used for the mass assemblies of the SA, SS and Hitler Youth, and was designed to hold large numbers of marching men. It also contained the Hall of Honour war memorial.
The Zeppelin Field had a grandstand designed by Albert Speer and modelled on the Pergamon Altar. It was used for mass parades and for Hitler's appearance before the party's formations.
The Congress Hall was begun but never completed, and the German Stadium was planned but barely begun, which shows how much grander the grounds were meant to become.
Albert Speer was the young architect who designed the grounds and staging and won Hitler's favour.
Staging used monumental stone architecture, huge swastika banners and eagles, massed standards, torchlight processions, bands and drums. The scale made each individual feel part of something vast.

The 'cathedral of light' was Speer's ring of anti-aircraft searchlights pointed into the night sky around the Zeppelin Field. Sources give about 130 to 150 lights, and it was used in the mid- to late 1930s rallies.
notes.tip: Keep the places apart: Luitpold Arena (SA and SS, war memorial), Zeppelin Field (Speer's grandstand, cathedral of light) and the unfinished Congress Hall. Do not confuse the architect Speer with Streicher, the Gauleiter of Franconia.

notes.h: Case study: the rallies in order, 1933-1939
notes.b: Each year's rally was named for what the regime wanted to celebrate, so the sequence of themes follows the regime's own progress from takeover to expansion.
points: The 1933 rally in September, the first held after Hitler became Chancellor, was the Rally of Victory, celebrating the seizure of power, and it was filmed as Victory of Faith.

The September 1934 rally was the first after the Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934), when Röhm and the SA leadership were murdered. It was staged to show party, SA, SS, Labour Service and army united behind Hitler, and was filmed as Triumph of the Will.
The 1935 rally was the Rally of Freedom, celebrating the return of conscription (March 1935) and rearmament, which the regime presented as Germany breaking free of Versailles.
During that rally the Reichstag was summoned to Nuremberg and on 15 September 1935 passed the Nuremberg Laws, together with the Reich Flag Law that made the swastika flag the national flag.
The 1936 rally was the Rally of Honour, after the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936. The Four Year Plan was proclaimed at it, and Göring was put in charge in October 1936.
The 1937 rally was the Rally of Labour and included parades of workers and the Labour Service.

The 1938 rally was the Rally of Greater Germany, celebrating the Anschluss of March 1938. Hitler's closing speech attacked Czechoslovakia over the Sudetenland, only weeks before the Munich Agreement of 29-30 September 1938.
The 1939 Rally of Peace was planned but cancelled because of the invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 and the outbreak of war.
notes.tip: Do not give an official name for the 1934 rally. Remember it as the first after the Night of the Long Knives and as the rally filmed in Triumph of the Will.

notes.h: Case study: the programme and ritual
notes.b: A fixed programme of set pieces made each rally feel like a ritual of loyalty rather than a party meeting.
points: Days were set aside for particular groups: the political leaders, the Labour Service, the Hitler Youth, the SA and SS, and the armed forces, who had their own day. Hitler gave an opening proclamation and a closing speech, and there were parades through the old city.

At the Luitpold Arena in 1934 Hitler walked between the SA and SS ranks with Himmler (head of the SS) and Viktor Lutze (SA chief of staff after Röhm) to the war memorial. This staged a reassurance to the SA and an image of the new order after the purge.

In the consecration of the standards, Hitler touched new flags with the Blood Flag (Blutfahne), the banner said to have been carried in the Munich Putsch of November 1923. This linked the new banners to the party's own founding story.
Rituals included oaths of loyalty, and in 1934 the Labour Service marched with spades. Together with the banners they gave the rallies a quasi-religious atmosphere and a sense of sacred purpose.
The night-time ceremonies, such as the political leaders' assembly under the cathedral of light and the torchlight processions, were the most dramatic part of the programme.
Hitler's speeches expressed party doctrine and foreign policy, which is why the rallies were also used to announce policies, as the Four Year Plan was in 1936.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level long answers on the rallies reward the programme and the ritual: the Blood Flag, the Luitpold Arena walk and the cathedral of light.

notes.b: What the rallies meant depended on who was there and who was watching. Participants, foreign diplomats and journalists left very different accounts, and the exam uses them as documents.
points: Hundreds of thousands of party members, workers, soldiers and youths came by special trains and lived in huge tent camps.
The camps ran under strict rules, such as passes to leave the grounds, fire safety, silence at night and the reporting of sickness, so that large numbers could be controlled.
Days were long, with drilling, marching and waiting. For many it was a powerful experience of comradeship and belonging, while for others it was exhausting.
Participants were organised into units and marched in disciplined formations, which created a visual impression of unity and order.
German participants showed enthusiasm, and foreign visitors and journalists were impressed too, some seeing evidence of the order and vitality of the new Germany.

William Shirer, an American correspondent, saw the 1934 rally and wrote about it in Berlin Diary (1941). Charles Bewley, Irish Minister (envoy) in Berlin from 1933 to 1939, was sympathetic to the regime.
Nevile Henderson, British ambassador to Germany from 1937, called the searchlight display a 'cathedral of ice', a phrase that echoes the 'cathedral of light' but with ice instead of light.
notes.tip: In a documents question, judge each source by who wrote it, when, why and with what attitude to the regime. For criticism, say whether a diplomat's, journalist's or participant's account is objective and what a photograph or camp rule sheet cannot show.

notes.h: Case study: purpose, reach and afterwards
notes.b: The rallies were staged for several purposes at once, and their reach went far beyond Nuremberg. Their afterlife shows how the city has dealt with that past.
points: The purpose was to display unity, order and strength, to build the Hitler cult and to bind the individual to the national community, which is why everyone marched, sang and swore oaths together.
Policies were announced at the rallies, including the Nuremberg Laws, the Four Year Plan and foreign policy claims, so racial ideas were presented as part of the national community.
The rallies also aimed to impress and intimidate foreign opinion by showing a disciplined, rearming Germany.
Radio, newsreels, the press and Riefenstahl's films carried the rallies to millions who never attended, and the films reached cinemas in Germany and abroad.
In April 1945 the US Army blew up the swastika on the Zeppelin Field grandstand. After 1945 the grounds were used by the US Army and the city, and parts of the Zeppelin Field survive today.
The Nuremberg war crimes trials (1945-46) were held in the city partly for its symbolism.
The unfinished Congress Hall now holds a Documentation Centre, which opened in 2001.
notes.tip: For cause and result questions, state why the regime staged the rallies and controlled the media, and what resulted (the Hitler cult, the publicising of racial law, foreign impressions), each with a specific example and a date.

notes.h: Assessment: the effectiveness and limits of Nazi propaganda
notes.b: Judgements of Nazi propaganda weigh its success in creating consent and loyalty against its limits, and ask how far it explains support for the regime.
points: Achievement: the Hitler cult and genuine popularity in the 1930s, the rallies' spectacle and the films' reach gave the regime a powerful image of unity.
Limit: propaganda failed to win over many workers and churchgoers, and it depended on terror, so the police, courts and camps were needed to suppress opposition.

Limit: people tired of constant political content, which is why so much of the media was entertainment, and after 1943 propaganda focused on defence and national survival, and its credibility fell as the war turned against Germany.

Contemporary view: many Germans responded with enthusiasm, and many foreigners were impressed, seeing awe-inspiring order and unity, while exiled opponents and foreign critics saw the rallies as an exhibition of dictatorship.

Later view: historians see manipulation and a link between the rallies, the racial laws and war, and Riefenstahl's films remain among the most studied examples of film propaganda and have shaped how later film-makers use visual rhetoric.

How far propaganda explains support: Ian Kershaw (The 'Hitler Myth', 1987) stresses that propaganda reinforced existing beliefs, and that economic recovery, foreign policy success, national pride and fear also mattered.
The reports of the exiled Social Democrats (Sopade) show grumbling and limits to belief, which is evidence that many people did not accept everything they were told.
Goebbels and Riefenstahl as contributors: Goebbels was the organiser who controlled what Germans saw and heard, while Riefenstahl was the artist who created the regime's most lasting images.
notes.tip: Use the judgement wording in questions: 'how effective', 'to what extent', 'achievements and limits'. Weigh enthusiasm against compulsion, entertainment against political content, and the 1930s peak against wartime decline, citing Kershaw and contemporary evidence such as Sopade reports.

The Nazi body set up in 1933 under Goebbels, through which artists, writers and journalists had to be admitted to work in Germany.

The annual Nazi party rally held in Nuremberg, staged as a demonstration of party unity and national strength.

The swastika banner said to have been carried in the 1923 Munich Putsch, used to consecrate new party flags at the rallies.
The speech of 18 February 1943 calling on Germans to accept total war after Stalingrad.
